label: Local Approach to the Monge Problem
notes: Chapter 10 spans printed pages 215 to 272 and solves the Monge problem a second time, now by a local method. Rather than convex analysis on Euclidean space, we read the optimal map straight off the first-order geometry of a cyclically monotone support, so the argument survives on a general Riemannian manifold.

label: From Kantorovich to a Map
notes: Recall the setting: a source measure absolutely continuous, a target measure, and a cost given by half the squared Riemannian distance. Kantorovich gives an optimal plan supported on a c-cyclically monotone set. The local approach asks when that support is actually a graph, so the plan collapses to a genuine transport map.

label: The c-Concave Potential
notes: Cyclical monotonicity packages the support inside the c-subdifferential of a c-concave potential psi. This potential is the manifold analogue of Brenier's convex function. Everything downstream is read from psi, so understanding how psi constrains destinations is the heart of the local method we develop here.

label: The Pointwise Selection Rule
notes: At a point x where psi is differentiable, the contact condition forces the gradient of the cost in its first slot to balance the gradient of psi. This is a stationarity equation: any destination y in the support must make the map of x plus the cost gradient vanish. It selects y from purely local data.

label: Twist and Single-Valued Maps
notes: The twist condition demands that fixing x and the cost gradient pins down a unique y. For the squared distance this holds away from the cut locus, where the exponential map is a diffeomorphism. Twist is exactly what turns the stationarity equation into a function rather than a set-valued relation.

label: Cost-Exponential Formula
notes: Inverting the twist relation gives the central formula. The destination is the Riemannian exponential of the gradient of psi at x. The gradient of the potential is the initial velocity of the minimizing geodesic running from x to its image, so the map is the time-one flow of that geodesic.

label: Reading the Map on a Manifold
notes: Walk the picture: at each source point the potential gradient is a tangent vector. Shoot the geodesic in that direction for unit time and you land at the destination. The whole transport map is this field of geodesics, recovering Brenier's straight-line transport when the manifold is flat Euclidean space.

label: Semiconcavity and Approximate Differentiability
notes: The squared distance is locally semiconcave, so psi inherits semiconcavity. By Alexandrov's theorem a semiconcave function is twice differentiable almost everywhere, hence approximately differentiable on a full-measure set. That regularity is the minimum needed to define the gradient that drives the cost-exponential formula.

label: The Cut Locus and Bad Sets
notes: Two obstructions live on negligible sets: points where psi fails to be differentiable, and points whose destination sits on the cut locus where the squared distance loses smoothness. Absolute continuity of the source gives these sets zero mass, so the formula holds almost everywhere and the gaps never carry transported mass.

label: McCann's Theorem
notes: Assembling the pieces yields McCann's theorem: for the quadratic cost on a Riemannian manifold with an absolutely continuous source, there is a unique optimal map, given by the cost-exponential of a c-concave potential's gradient. This is the manifold extension of Brenier's theorem, proven by the local method.

label: Uniqueness Almost Everywhere
notes: Uniqueness rests on absolute continuity. Where the source density is positive the selection rule is single-valued almost everywhere, so any two optimal maps agree off a null set. Drop absolute continuity and mass can split at non-differentiability points, and the map degenerates back into a genuine plan.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: The local approach trades global convexity for local first-order geometry, which is why it travels to manifolds and to general twisted costs. Keep three anchors: the c-concave potential, the stationarity equation, and the cost-exponential. These reappear when displacement interpolation and Ricci curvature bounds enter in later chapters.
